cards.heading: Infrastructure as code
cards.body: Configuration management tools describe the desired state of devices or infrastructure in files kept under version control. The tool makes reality match the files: repeatable, reviewable and consistent. Because the files are under version control, every change can be reviewed, repeated and rolled back. The tools aim to be idempotent: a task describes the end state, so re-running it changes nothing if it's already done and only acts where the device differs.

cards.heading: Ansible
cards.body: Agentless: nothing to install on devices. A control node pushes changes over SSH (or NETCONF/APIs). Inventory files list the devices; playbooks written in YAML list tasks that call modules (such as ios_config). Written in Python.
cards.example:
- name: Set NTP
  hosts: routers
  tasks:
    - cisco.ios.ios_config:
        lines:
          - ntp server 10.0.0.100

cards.heading: Terraform
cards.body: HashiCorp's infrastructure-as-code tool, declarative and written in HCL. It provisions infrastructure (cloud networks, VMs, controller objects) through providers. 'terraform plan' shows what will change; 'terraform apply' does it; a state file tracks what exists.

cards.heading: Puppet and Chef
cards.body: Older agent-based tools: an agent on each managed node pulls its configuration from a server. Puppet uses manifests in its own declarative language; Chef uses cookbooks and recipes in Ruby. They're less common for network devices, which can't run agents.

cards.heading: Push and pull
cards.body: Push: the controller sends changes when you run it (Ansible). Pull: agents on the nodes check in and fetch their configuration (Puppet, Chef). Declarative tools state the end result (Terraform, Puppet); procedural ones list the steps to take (Ansible playbooks run in order).
